title: Meteor Dust Creates Invisible Clouds That Bounce Radio Signals
mediaSource: NASA sporadic E metallic clouds radio signals sounding rocket

scenes.title: Invisible metallic clouds drift high above Earth
scenes.narration: High above Earth, thin layers made from vaporized meteor metals can form without being seen, yet they can strongly affect radio signals.

scenes.title: Burning meteors seed the upper atmosphere
scenes.narration: As meteors burn up, metallic material can collect at high altitude and form temporary layers called sporadic E.

scenes.title: Radio waves can bounce in unexpected directions
scenes.narration: When these layers appear, long-distance radio signals can reflect in surprising ways, suddenly changing communication conditions.

scenes.title: NASA sampled five points at once
scenes.narration: A NASA sounding rocket released multiple sensors so researchers could measure different parts of the same layer simultaneously.

scenes.title: The layer was more complex than expected
scenes.narration: The multi-point measurements showed the metallic layer was not a simple uniform sheet, with electrical properties changing from place to place.

scenes.title: Meteor leftovers can affect technology on the ground
scenes.narration: Tiny traces of meteors can gather high above Earth and change the paths of radio signals used far below.
